title: Danilo Souza
text:
Economia do Crime
  EAE1247 · Graduação
  Department of Economics, School of Economics, Business and Accounting (FEA-USP)
  Danilo Souza · 3 de Agosto - 30 de Novembro, 2026



  Plano de aulas e lista de artigos
  Office hours
  Email
  ← Todos as disciplinas







Nesta disciplina, o aluno é apresentado à análise econômica do crime. O curso parte do modelo canônico de escolha racional e atividade criminosa em equilíbrio parcial. A partir daí são apresentados artigos empíricos que discutem várias dimensões do modelo e questões não capturadas por ele. O objetivo central do curso é expor o aluno às discussões mais recentes em relação aos determinantes e efeitos da atividade criminosa nos mais diversos contextos e grupos sociais.



Alunos devem se sentir confortáveis com teoria microeconômica básica e econometria. Apesar de não obrigatório, conhecimento prévio a respeito de métodos modernos de identificação causal, como diferenças em diferenças, regressão descontínua e variáveis instrumentais é altamente recomendado.




Modelo de escolha racional e atividade criminosa

Modelo de custos e benefícios: Becker (1968)
Modelo de alocação de tempo: Ehrlich (1973)
Efeitos da alteração de custos diretos: Prisão, Punição e Policiamento
Efeitos da alteração nos custos de oportunidade: Mercado de Trabalho e Educação

Tópicos em Economia do Crime

Choques econômicos e equilíbrio geral
Crimes ambientais
Fiscalização e monitoramento
Imigração
Capital social e redes
Crime organizado
Drogas e mercados ilegais







Lecture Notes - Danilo Souza
Buonanno, P., P. Vanin, and J. Vargas (2022). A Modern Guide to the Economics of Crime. Cheltenham, UK: Edward Elgar Publishing.
Chalfin, A. and J. McCrary (2017). Criminal deterrence: a review of the literature. Journal of Economic Literature, Vol. 55 (No. 1), pp. 5–48.
Draca, M. and S. Machin (2015). Crime and economic incentives. Annual Review of Economics, Vol. 7, pp. 389–408.











Segunda-feira às 7:30–9:10 PM e Quarta-feira às 9:20–11:00 PM
Sala A-5 (segunda-feira) e A-8 (quarta-feira) do FEA-1
3 de Agosto - 30 de Novembro, 2026








A avaliação do curso consiste em presença em aula (peso 5%), uma prova intermediária (peso 30%), uma apresentação de artigo acadêmico a ser realizada nas datas indicadas no plano de aulas (peso 45%) e dois quizzes surpresa sobre o conteúdo das apresentações (20%). Apenas os alunos que não atingirem a média 5 serão submetidos à prova de reavaliação, assim como consta no regimento da faculdade.
Os grupos deverão ser compostos por 3 alunos cada. Os grupos terão 35min para apresentar e todos os membros do grupo devem estar presentes. O membro do grupo que não comparecer à aula de apresentação terá sua nota zerada.




Prova intermediária: 23 de Setembro
Definição dos grupos até 14 de Setembro. Nesse mesmo dia será liberada a escolha dos artigos.









Dúvidas não resolvidas durante a aula devem ser sanadas, preferencialmente, durante o horário de atendimento na minha sala. Dúvidas específicas (e que podem ser resumidas em poucas linhas) devem ser encaminhadas ao meu e-mail com o assunto EAE1247 - NomeSobrenome, substituindo o campo NomeSobrenome pelo seu primeiro nome seguido do último sobrenome. Fora isso, sintam-se a vontade para me acessar, pessoalmente ou via e-mail, para tratar de qualquer outro assunto.

I’m an Associate Professor of Economics at the School of Economics, Business and Accounting at the University of São Paulo (FEA-USP).
My research interests are primarily in the Economics of Crime and Labor Economics. I am interested in how economic shocks and institutions shape crime, in how crime in turn affects firms and labor market outcomes, and in how legal institutions affect labor markets. I am also interested in organized crime and its links to the formal economy and to institutions in Brazil.

title: Danilo Souza
text:
Economics of Crime I
  EAE6089 · Graduate
  Department of Economics, School of Economics, Business and Accounting (FEA-USP)
  Danilo Souza · August 3 - October 11, 2026



  Lecture Plan and Reading List
  Referee Report List
  Office hours
  Email
  ← All courses






This course prepares students to engage critically with the economics of crime, with an emphasis on empirical research that uses modern methods of causal identification. We cover the effects of policing, punishment, labor market conditions, and education on crime, as well as public policy in illegal markets and the dynamics of organized crime. Students will learn to assess the existing evidence, identify gaps in the literature, and design original projects with the potential for high-impact publication.



Students should be comfortable with microeconomic theory — in particular the analysis of market failures and welfare — and with modern methods of causal identification, including differences-in-differences, regression discontinuity, and instrumental variables. Prior coursework in econometrics is strongly recommended.




Motivation: data, the state of the field, and empirical challenges
The rational choice model: static and dynamics
Policing, enforcement, and discrimination
Incarceration, monitoring, and punishment
Labour market conditions and education
Organised crime: causes and consequences
Illegal markets and drugs

A detailed reading list for each topic is available above.







Mondays and Wednesdays, 4:00–5:50 PM
Room A-8, FEA I Building
August 3 - October 11, 2026






Assessment has three components: (i) a referee report on an unpublished paper, (ii) a class presentation of a published paper, and (iii) an original research project on a topic related to the course, submitted as a 10–15 page paper and presented in class. The first two are worth 20% each; the project accounts for the remaining 60%.




Referee report due on 11 September
Research project presentations: 23 & 28 September
Final research project due on 9 October





AI tools are not prohibited, but they must not form the basis of your work: the analysis, the interpretation, and the ideas must be yours. This course follows the standards now set by academic publishers, and you are strongly encouraged to read both — they are short, and you will be held to them when you submit your own papers: Elsevier and Wiley.
Every submission in which AI was used must close with a section titled “Declaration of generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the [referee report / manuscript] preparation process”, stating exactly which tool was used and at which stages. Use the templates provided by either publisher. Basic spelling and grammar checks need not be declared.
When writing your referee report, never upload the paper, or any part of it, into an AI tool. An unpublished manuscript is a confidential document, and doing so may violate the authors’ confidentiality and proprietary rights.
Don’t get me wrong, AI is a remarkable tool, and it raises productivity on routine tasks — but leaning on it too heavily, at the expense of how we have traditionally studied and learned, may damage the learning process itself and erode our ability to recognize what we do not know. The evidence increasingly points in this direction. In the working paper “The Generative AI Learning Penalty: Evidence from Chinese Secondary Education”, Strömberg, Lei, and Wu track 26,811 students over 30 months and find that AI adoption raised homework productivity: scores rose by 18% while completion time fell by 30%. On the other hand, scores on closed-book exams, a common measure of learning outcome, decreased by 20% within six months. The losses are concentrated among the students whose short completion times and high homework scores indicate they had outsourced the work, while those who kept putting in the hours lost almost nothing. The Economist covered the paper here. The figure below shows the size of the problem and the challenge that we will have to face in the coming years.






Figure 1









Questions that come up during class are best resolved in class. For anything that remains, please come to office hours. Short questions — ones that fit in a few lines — can be sent by email with the subject line EAE6089 — FirstnameLastname. Beyond that, feel free to reach out in person or by email about anything else.
